title: Question-Asking Audit: Rate Your Own Questioning
description: A short, honest self-audit that shows you the kinds of questions you actually ask in class — not the kinds you think you ask. Most teachers are surprised to learn how much of their questioning sits at the recall level.
howTo:
Record one full class period, or ask a colleague to sit in and jot down every question you ask, word for word.
Afterward, sort each question into a level — Knowledge/recall, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis, or Evaluation — using a simple tally sheet.
Total each column and calculate the percentage of your questions that landed at the bottom two levels versus the top four.
Note which parts of the lesson pulled you toward recall questions (checking homework, reviewing vocabulary) and which parts opened room for higher-level ones (discussion, analysis of a text or problem).
Repeat the audit again in a few weeks on a different lesson type to see whether the balance shifts once you're watching for it.
example: A teacher records a 50-minute lesson and tallies 34 questions asked that day. Sorting them afterward, 27 fall into the recall/knowledge category ("What year did this happen?" "What's the definition?") and only 7 reach analysis or above — a pattern the teacher had no idea was that lopsided until seeing it in writing.
sourceName: Chicago Center for Teaching and Learning, University of Chicago

title: Inquiry-Based Learning
description: Spark curiosity with targeted questions, then give students time to research and lead their own exploration.
howTo: Open a unit with a compelling question instead of an answer. Provide time for student-led research and structure a class discussion around what they discover.
example: Instead of announcing the definition of natural selection, the teacher opens a biology unit by showing students photos of peppered moths on sooty versus clean tree bark and asks, "Why did the population's color change over fifty years?" Students spend fifteen minutes in small groups generating hypotheses and researching using provided data tables before the class discussion builds toward the formal explanation of natural selection. The teacher only introduces the vocabulary term after students have argued through the mechanism themselves.
videoTitle: Inquiry Learning in the Classroom
sourceName: Instructure

title: Activate Prior Knowledge
description: Connect the day's topic to knowledge students already possess before they read, so they can link old and new ideas.
howTo: Open with a quick brainstorm or turn-and-talk: 'What do you already know about X?' before introducing new text or content on that topic.
example: Before starting a unit on ecosystems, the teacher opens with a turn-and-talk: "What do you already know about food chains from earlier grades?" Students share what they remember about predators and prey, and the teacher uses their answers to bridge into new vocabulary like "decomposer" and "trophic level."
videoTitle: Leveraging Prior Knowledge to Build Understanding
sourceName: Branching Minds

title: Reciprocal Questioning
description: When introducing a new topic, have students describe the concept back in their own words through structured Q&A.
howTo: Pair students and give each a role: one asks a question about the new concept, the other answers in their own words, then they switch.
example: After introducing the concept of supply and demand, the teacher pairs students and gives one the role of asking a question about the concept ("What happens to price when supply drops?") while the other answers in their own words before they switch roles. Each pair must generate at least three question-answer rounds before rejoining the whole class. The teacher listens in on a few pairs to catch students who are only reciting the definition rather than explaining the mechanism.
videoTitle: LEAP: Reciprocal Questioning
sourceName: Instructure

title: Question Formulation Technique (QFT)
description: A simple, repeatable protocol that hands question-asking over to students: give them a focus (an image, statement, or phenomenon) and a short list of rules, and let them generate, refine, and prioritize their own questions before you teach a thing.
howTo:
Design a Question Focus — a single provocative image, statement, or short phenomenon related to the topic (not a question itself).
Review the four rules with students: ask as many questions as you can, do not stop to discuss or answer any question, write down every question exactly as stated, change any statement into a question.
Give small groups a set time (5-8 minutes) to produce as many questions as possible from the Question Focus, recording every one.
Have groups label each question as open-ended or closed-ended, then practice changing a few from one type to the other.
Ask each group to prioritize their top 2-3 questions to investigate further, and use those to drive the lesson or unit that follows.
example: Before starting a unit on fractions, a fourth-grade teacher shows students a visual of a partially shaded circle with no explanation. Groups generate questions like "Why is part of it shaded?" and "Can we make our own fractions out of it?", then choose their top three questions to guide the next few days of instruction.
videoTitle: Using the Question Formulation Technique (QFT) for Formative Assessment
sourceName: Right Question Institute

title: The Difference Between Difficulty and Rigor
description: Rigor does not mean making work harder — it means balancing difficulty and complexity so every student is taught up to genuinely high expectations. Confusing the two leads to piling on more work or more obscure vocabulary instead of asking students to think more deeply.
howTo:
Sort a recent week of assignments into four types: fluency tasks (not difficult or complex, but keep a needed skill sharp), stamina tasks (not complex, but take sustained time and effort), strategic-thinking tasks (complex but not overly difficult once modeled), and struggle tasks (both complex and difficult, requiring real grappling).
Check whether your week leaned almost entirely on fluency and stamina tasks — a common trap that feels rigorous because it's effortful, but isn't complex.
For one lesson, deliberately design a strategic-thinking task: give students a problem or text that requires reasoning, provide the modeling and support they need to access it, and resist the urge to make it 'harder' by adding length or obscurity instead of depth.
Reserve true struggle tasks for moments where the productive grappling itself is the point — a close reading of a hard passage, a project requiring synthesis — not as a daily default.
example: A 4th-grade teacher realizes that this week's "rigorous" reading assignments were really just longer passages with harder vocabulary — a difficulty increase, not a complexity increase. The next week, she keeps the same reading level but adds a strategic-thinking task: students must find and defend the one sentence in the passage that changes the story's meaning most, a complex task that doesn't require harder vocabulary to be genuinely more rigorous.
videoTitle: Redefining Rigor in the Classroom
sourceName: ASCD Educational Leadership — "Rigor Is More Than Hard Work" (Fisher & Frey)

title: Notice & Wonder
description: An entry routine where students observe a stripped-down graph, table, or image and generate their own notices and wonders, letting the class author the day's mathematical question and lowering the risk of entering the discussion.
howTo:
Project a mathematical object (graph, table, or photo) with every question and label beyond axes stripped away.
Give students 1 minute of silent writing for notices (observations only), then 1 minute for wonders (questions the object raises).
Harvest every offer onto the board verbatim without judgment, notices then wonders (4 minutes).
Let the class pick the wonder worth chasing, steering only if the target doesn't surface (2 minutes).
Post the chosen wonder as the lesson's purpose question for the rest of the period; park any wonder the teacher is tempted to answer immediately instead of answering it on the spot.
example: The teacher projects the stripped two-line phone-plan graph with no labels beyond the axes and no explanation. Students spend one minute writing only what they notice ("two lines," "they cross," "one starts higher") and one minute writing what they wonder ("why would anyone pick the plan that starts higher?" "where exactly do they cross?"), and every offer is harvested onto the board verbatim with no judgment. The class then picks the wonder worth chasing — usually something like "which plan is cheaper, and does it depend on how long you keep it?" — and that question, in the students' own words, becomes the posted purpose for the lesson.
videoTitle: Spark curiosity with a “Notice and Wonder” math routine
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Notice & Wonder the Phenomenon
description: An entry routine that opens a unit with a stripped-down, unexplained phenomenon so every student can begin with low-risk observation before being asked to explain or defend anything.
howTo:
Show the real phenomenon live or on a short video with no labels, explanation, or vocabulary.
Give students 2 minutes to silently write only what they notice — observations, no explanations.
Give students 2 minutes to write what they wonder.
Harvest both lists verbatim on the board with no judgment (4 minutes).
Have the class choose the wonder worth chasing and post it as the unit's investigation question (2 minutes).
example: The teacher sets two identical ice cubes on a metal block and a foam block at the same moment, with no labels or explanation, and gives students two minutes to silently write only what they notice, such as "the metal one melted faster" or "there's a puddle under the metal one first." After harvesting notices and wonders on the board verbatim, the class chooses the wonder worth chasing — "why does ice melt faster on the metal when metal feels colder?" — and posts it as the unit's investigation question.
videoTitle: Notice and Wonder | Iowa Science Phenomena
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Which One Doesn't Belong
description: A low-risk classification activity using a 2x2 grid of related items where every item can be defended as the outlier, shifting the challenge from choosing correctly to defending precisely with mathematical vocabulary.
howTo:
Present four related items (equations, graphs, or numbers) arranged so each one could defensibly be the outlier for a different reason.
Give students 1 minute of silent time to pick an outlier and write a reason.
Have students group by their choice and defend it using precise vocabulary such as slope, intercept, or constant (5 minutes).
Reveal that all choices are valid and shift the discussion to what distinguishes a strong defense; rank two defenses as a class (3 minutes).
Require at least one Tier 3 vocabulary word in any defense to count, preventing surface-level justifications.
example: The teacher posts a 2x2 grid of four related linear equations — y = 20m + 30, y = 22m + 10, y = 20m − 5, y = 30 — built so every item can be defended as the outlier for a different reason. Students silently pick their outlier and write a reason, then defend their choice in corners using vocabulary like slope, intercept, and rate; the teacher reveals that every choice is defensible and pushes the class to rank two defenses by precision, since 'it looks different' scores lower than 'it's the only one with no rate term, so its graph is flat.' Students then upgrade their own written defense once, replacing a surface observation with a defense grounded in slope, intercept, and consequence.
videoTitle: Strengthen math thinking with a “Which One Doesn't Belong” routine
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Question Types Toolkit: Convergent, Divergent, and Beyond
description: Build your own working inventory of question types so you can reach for the right one in the moment instead of defaulting to whatever comes to mind. Convergent questions narrow toward one defensible answer; divergent questions open toward many.
howTo:
Learn the core distinction first: convergent questions ask students to bring together evidence or ideas and converge on a single logical conclusion ("Based on the data, which plan is cheaper after 6 months?"); divergent questions have no single answer and invite multiple valid responses ("What are all the ways this character could have responded?").
Add a few more tools to the kit: probing questions (follow-ups that push for justification — "What in the text makes you say that?"), hypothetical questions ("What if this variable changed?"), and application questions ("Where would this show up outside of class?").
Before a lesson, plan at least one convergent and one divergent question tied to the same content so you can pivot depending on how discussion is going.
During class, notice which type you default to under pressure — most teachers over-rely on convergent, closed questions when time feels short — and deliberately insert a divergent one to reopen thinking.
example: Discussing a short story's ending, the teacher first asks a convergent question — "What single piece of evidence best explains why the character stays silent?" — then follows with a divergent one — "What are all the different reasons she might have had, even ones the text doesn't fully confirm?" — giving both a settled answer and room for genuine debate.
videoTitle: 18 Types of Questions for Teachers [Enhance Your Questioning Repertoire]
sourceName: Jonathan Sandling — 18 Types of Questions Teachers Can Ask in Lessons

title: Using Revised Bloom's Taxonomy to Improve Your Questioning
description: The revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create) gives you six rungs to climb with any content. Planning at least one question per level — not just the bottom two — is what actually raises the ceiling of a lesson.
howTo:
Remember: recall a fact, term, or step. Reading/ELA — "What is the setting of the story?" Math — "What is the formula for area of a rectangle?" Science — "What are the three states of matter?" Social Studies — "In what year did the event occur?"
Understand: explain it in your own words. Reading/ELA — "Summarize the main conflict in your own words." Math — "Explain why we multiply length by width to get area." Science — "Describe what happens to water molecules as ice melts." Social Studies — "Explain why the treaty was signed."
Apply: use it in a new situation. Reading/ELA — "Use the vocabulary word correctly in a new sentence about your own life." Math — "Find the area of your classroom floor using this formula." Science — "Predict what would happen if you heated the ice cube faster." Social Studies — "Apply this cause-and-effect pattern to a different historical event."
Analyze: break it into parts and find relationships. Reading/ELA — "Compare how two characters respond to the same conflict." Math — "What patterns do you notice between the shapes' areas and perimeters?" Science — "What factors caused one block's ice to melt faster than the other's?" Social Studies — "What economic and political factors combined to cause the event?"
Evaluate: make a judgment using criteria. Reading/ELA — "Which character's choice was more justified, and why?" Math — "Which method for solving this problem is most efficient, and why?" Science — "How convincing is this data as evidence for the claim?" Social Studies — "Was the treaty a fair resolution? Defend your answer."
Create: produce something new. Reading/ELA — "Write an alternate ending that changes one character's choice." Math — "Design a word problem that requires this formula to solve." Science — "Design an experiment to test your prediction." Social Studies — "Draft a proposal for how the conflict could have been resolved differently."
example: Planning a single lesson on ecosystems, a teacher writes one question at each level in advance — recall ("name a producer and a consumer"), understand ("explain the role of decomposers in your own words"), apply ("predict what happens to the food web if the producers disappear"), analyze ("compare two food webs and explain which is more resilient"), evaluate ("which food web is healthier, and what evidence supports that"), create ("design a food web for a new environment") — so the lesson climbs instead of staying flat.
videoTitle: Bloom's Taxonomy: Effective Questioning
sourceName: Chicago Center for Teaching and Learning, University of Chicago — Sample Question Tool Kit

title: Golden Line
description: A quick activity converting a vague 'I liked it' into the smallest complete act of literary argument: every student picks one line the text cannot lose and defends what would be lost if it were cut.
howTo:
Give students 3 minutes to choose their golden line and write why it does something no other line does.
Have students stand and share around the room: the line, its paragraph number, and one sentence of why, with no repeats unless a new reason is added (5 minutes).
Cluster the picks on the board and discuss where the room converged and what that reveals about the story (4 minutes).
If everyone picks the famous last line, retire it after three picks and require students to find another load-bearing line.
example: After reading "The Story of an Hour," a student picks "she had loved him — sometimes" (paragraph 13) as their golden line, writing that without it Louise becomes "easy — either a victim or a villain," since that one word forces the reader to hold two true things at once. Students share their lines and paragraph numbers around the room with no repeats unless a new reason is added, and the teacher retires the famous last line after three picks so students find other load-bearing lines.
videoTitle: Using Golden Lines When Reading
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Say It Two Ways
description: A performance-based activity converting tone from a matter of taste into an evidence-based argument by having pairs perform a loaded line two plausible ways, then use surrounding text to rule one reading out.
howTo:
Choose lines whose meaning depends heavily on tone and give one line per pair.
Give pairs 3 minutes to rehearse the line in two different, both-plausible tones.
Have pairs perform both versions for another pair (3 minutes).
Have pairs find the surrounding words in the text that rule one version out and argue which reading the text actually supports (4 minutes).
Have students write an exit sentence: 'Our line means ___ because the text around it says "___".'
If students treat tone as pure taste, enforce the surrounding-words rule: a tone claim must cite the words that produce it.
example: A pair rehearses Josephine's line "you will make yourself ill" from "The Story of an Hour" two ways — once sounding genuinely worried, once sounding controlling — then performs both versions for another pair. They argue that the surrounding words, where Josephine is "imploring for admission" while Louise is "drinking in a very elixir of life," support the controlling reading, and write the exit sentence naming the tone and the words that produced it.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: The Editor's Cut
description: An activity framing students as anthology editors who must nominate a paragraph to cut and defend or rescue that decision, teaching structural reading by forcing students to name exactly what a paragraph is doing.
howTo:
Present the premise: an anthology editor demands the story lose one paragraph, and the class must decide which cut does least damage.
Give pairs 5 minutes to nominate the most cuttable paragraph and write a defense of what the story loses and why it survives.
Post nominations on the board; for each, have one pair argue for the cut and another argue for the rescue, naming what the cutters missed (6 minutes).
Discuss the likely finding that nothing cuts cleanly, and name why: in compressed fiction, every paragraph is load-bearing (2 minutes).
Have students write an exit sentence naming the paragraph they'd fight hardest to keep and why.
If students argue for cutting based on boredom, enforce the damage rule: a cut must be argued by what remains, not by what feels slow.
example: Framed as anthology editors, pairs nominate the most cuttable paragraph of "The Story of an Hour" and defend the cut, and another pair argues to rescue it — for instance, arguing that cutting the weeping paragraph would make Louise look heartless since her grief has to be real for her later freedom to feel complicated. The class usually finds nothing cuts cleanly, naming that in compressed fiction every paragraph is load-bearing, and each student writes which paragraph they'd fight hardest to keep.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Gallery of Methods
description: An activity where the teacher selects and sequences several genuinely different correct student solution methods for the class to compare, helping students find the same underlying mathematics across different representations.
howTo:
While students solve, circulate and select three or four genuinely different correct or instructive methods (graph, table, equation, estimate-and-adjust), sequencing them from concrete to abstract; ask student permission before posting.
Have students do a silent gallery read of all posted methods (3 minutes).
In pairs, have students identify what is the same underneath the differences and find one method hiding inside another (5 minutes).
Facilitate a class discussion on which method would break first with uglier numbers and which generalizes (5 minutes).
Close with an exit prompt: 'The method I didn't use that I now understand is ___, and it works because ___' (2 minutes).
example: While students solve the phone-plan break-even problem, the teacher selects three or four genuinely different correct methods — a graph, a table, an equation, and an estimate-and-adjust approach — sequencing them from concrete to abstract and posting them numbered. Pairs do a silent gallery read, then discuss what's the same underneath the different-looking methods, hunting for the table hiding inside the graph and the equation hiding inside the table. Each student closes with an exit sentence like 'the method I didn't use that I now understand is the table, because each row is just the equation evaluated at one month, and the break-even is where the columns swap order.'
videoTitle: A Gallery Walk to Inspire Student Collaboration (Early Math Collaborative)
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Gallery of Readings
description: A gallery-walk activity displaying several genuinely different anonymous student readings so students can compare what evidence each reading stands on, transferring ownership of interpretation beyond the original writer.
howTo:
While students draft, circulate and select three or four genuinely different defensible readings; ask permission and post them numbered with names removed.
Give students 3 minutes for a silent gallery read of all the readings.
In pairs, have students discuss what evidence each reading stands on and where two readings use the same line differently (5 minutes).
As a class, discuss which reading would be hardest to defend against a complicating passage and which reading generalizes the furthest (5 minutes).
Have students write an exit sentence naming a reading they didn't write that they now understand, with its best evidence.
example: While students draft Reader's Paragraphs on "The Story of an Hour," the teacher posts three anonymous, genuinely different readings — the marriage-indictment reading, the sympathetic-Josephine reading, and the irony-of-medicine reading. Pairs discuss what evidence each reading stands on, noting how two readings can use the same last line, "of joy that kills," differently, and each student writes an exit sentence naming a reading they didn't write but now understand.
videoTitle: Gallery Walk - Classroom Strategy
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Mystery Document
description: Students examine a visually rich source with its caption removed, building an evidence-based hypothesis about who made it, when, and why before the answer is revealed — lowering the risk of entering a lesson and rewarding observation over guessing.
howTo:
Strip a visually rich source (photo, map, ledger page, cartoon) of every caption, date, and credit.
Give students 2 minutes of silent noticing, listing only observations, not interpretations.
Have pairs merge lists and sort into observed vs. inferred (3 minutes).
Run rounds where each pair offers one observation and one inference tied to a visible detail (5 minutes); the class drafts source guesses tied to details (5 minutes).
Reveal the caption and compare, discussing which detail carried the most information (3 minutes).
Have each student write a three-line source hypothesis and reconcile it with the reveal.
example: The teacher projects an allotment-era map with its caption stripped away and gives students two silent minutes to list only observations, such as a perfect numbered grid with handwritten names filling the squares. Pairs sort their observations into observed versus inferred, offer a source hypothesis tied to a specific detail, and only then does the teacher reveal that it is a Dawes-era allotment map, letting the class check how close their reasoning came.
videoTitle: Analyzing Primary and Secondary Sources in a Middle School Classroom
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Mystery Text
description: An entry-point activity that strips a passage of title, author, and context so students notice and hypothesize before interpreting, making the interpretive question arrive before the plot and lowering the risk of a first guess.
howTo:
Choose a short passage and strip everything around it: title, author, date, even the course.
Give students 2 minutes of silent noticing to list what the sentence does — who speaks, what's strange, what's missing.
Give pairs 4 minutes to merge lists and draft hypotheses about what kind of story or text this must be from.
In rounds, have each pair offer one hypothesis tied to one specific word in the line (5 minutes).
Reveal the title and first sentence only, and have students revise their hypotheses in writing (4 minutes) before reading the full text.
If students guess with no textual anchor, enforce the one-word rule: every hypothesis must name the word it stands on, or it waits.
example: The teacher projects only the final line of "The Story of an Hour" — "When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease — of joy that kills" — with no title, author, or story attached. Students spend two minutes silently noticing what the sentence does, then pairs draft hypotheses about what kind of story ends this way, tying each guess to one specific word like "they said," before the title is revealed and they revise their hypotheses in writing.
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Numberless Word Problem
description: A staged-reveal activity that strips all numbers from a word problem so students must reason about structure and identify the hidden quantity before any calculation is possible, resetting who counts as 'good at math.'
howTo:
Rewrite the day's word problem with every number removed, leaving only the structure.
Post the numberless version and have pairs discuss the situation, what matters, and what's hidden (4 minutes).
Harvest as a class: have students name the quantity that will decide the problem before any number exists (3 minutes).
Reveal the numbers and have pairs predict what kind of answer is coming (3 minutes).
Reveal the question last, compare it to predictions, then dissect and solve with the structure already understood (5 minutes).
example: The teacher strips all numbers from the phone-plan problem, posting only: 'A phone company offers two plans. One costs more to start but less each month. The other costs less to start but more each month.' Pairs discuss what matters and what's hidden before any calculation is possible, and the class names the hidden quantity — how long you keep the phone — before a single number exists. Only after that structural conversation does the teacher reveal the dollar amounts, then finally the question itself, and pairs compare their predicted answer shape ('a plan and a condition') against what they actually find.
videoTitle: Intro to Numberless Word Problems
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Data Talk (Numberless Graph)
description: A staged graph-reveal routine that shows axes, then shapes, then values in sequence, training students to read a graph's story and meaning before jumping to specific data points.
howTo:
Reveal only the axes and labels first; have pairs discuss what the graph could be about and what a point would mean (3 minutes).
Add the curves with no numbers and have pairs discuss which is faster and where something changes (5 minutes).
Add the numbers and have pairs write the one sentence the graph is arguing (4 minutes).
Discuss as a class the landmark feature (e.g., a plateau) and what it means (3 minutes).
example: The teacher reveals the ice-melting graph in stages: first just the axes, prompting pairs to guess what the graph could be about, then the two curves with no numbers so students discuss which line is faster and where something changes, then finally the numbers. Students end by writing the one sentence the graph argues and identifying the landmark feature — the metal curve's plateau at 5 minutes, meaning the ice is entirely gone rather than that melting slowed down.
videoTitle: Developing & nurturing data literacy using slow reveal graphs ...
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: The Dissection Protocol (Four-Pass Data Table Read)
description: A repeatable four-pass routine for reading a data table that separates measurement, pattern, inference, and follow-up testing, teaching students to treat data as a text with a story rather than a list of numbers to copy.
howTo:
Pass 1: Read the columns aloud — identify what was measured, in what units, and how often, naming the independent, dependent, and controlled variables precisely.
Pass 2: Find the shape — run a finger along each row to describe its trend in one phrase (e.g., 'fast then flat' vs. 'slow and steady').
Pass 3: Separate observation from inference — mark what the table actually states versus what students are tempted to add as a conclusion.
Pass 4: Ask what would test it — have a student propose a check, such as running it again or identifying another difference between conditions.
example: On the ice-melting data table, Pass 1 has students read the columns aloud, naming block material as the independent variable and percent melted as the dependent variable measured every minute. Pass 2 has them run a finger along each row to find the shape — metal is fast then flat by minute 5, foam is slow and steady until minute 9 — Pass 3 separates the measured fact that metal reached 100% from the inference that "metal is hotter," and Pass 4 has a student propose running the trial again to test it.
videoTitle: Help students Read and Interpret Data Tables in four simple steps
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Reading a Graph as a Text
description: A four-step protocol (frame, units/scale, shape, landmarks) that teaches students to read a graph systematically instead of jumping straight to its numbers, building genuine graphical literacy.
howTo:
Frame: identify what is on each axis, saying it aloud in words before anything else.
Units & scale: determine what one gridline equals and whether the graph starts at zero.
Shape: describe the overall story at arm's length (rising, falling, straight, bending, crossing) with no numbers yet.
Landmarks: name the points that matter — intercepts, intersections, peaks — in words before translating them into sentences or computation.
example: Given the graph of two crossing phone-plan cost lines, students work through four questions in order rather than jumping to numbers: Frame ('months across, dollars up'), Units & Scale (what one gridline equals, and whether the axis starts at zero), Shape (one line starts higher but climbs more slowly, so they must cross), and Landmarks (the exact intersection point, named in words as 'they cross at ten months' before any values are pulled from it). Only after narrating the shape and landmarks aloud do students move to pulling specific data points, which prevents the common error of reading isolated values with no sense of the overall story the graph is telling.
videoTitle: Teaching Graphing & Data in First Grade, Literacy Curriculum ...
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Reading the Cognitive Level Baked Into a Standard (DOK)
description: Every content standard already has a cognitive ceiling built into its verb and its task — Webb's Depth of Knowledge (DOK) gives you a way to name that ceiling and decide whether to push above it.
howTo:
Read the standard and identify its core verb and task, then classify it: DOK 1 (recall and reproduction — facts, definitions, one-step procedures), DOK 2 (skills and concepts — compare, organize, interpret, summarize, requiring more than one step), DOK 3 (strategic thinking — reason, plan, use evidence, justify, draw conclusions), or DOK 4 (extended thinking — investigate, synthesize across sources, extended projects).
Remember that DOK is not the same as difficulty — a DOK 1 task can still be hard if the content is unfamiliar, and a DOK 3 task can be accessible if it's well scaffolded.
If a standard's verb sounds low ("identify," "list") but the intent of the unit is deeper, design the actual classroom task at the higher DOK level the standard is really asking for — the verb is a floor, not a ceiling.
When an assignment has multiple parts, code the whole task at its highest DOK level, even if only one part reaches that level.
example: A standard reads "identify the causes of the event" — a verb that sounds like simple recall (DOK 1). Recognizing that genuinely explaining multiple interacting causes requires reasoning and evidence, the teacher designs the actual task at DOK 3: students must rank the causes by importance and defend the ranking with cited evidence, not just list them.
videoTitle: Identifying Webb's Depth of Knowledge Levels
sourceName: Idaho Training Clearinghouse — Depth of Knowledge (Norman Webb)

title: Writing Rigorous Questions: A Stem Bank by Bloom's Level
description: Having a stem bank on hand when you sit down to write an assignment or assessment makes it far easier to include higher-order items instead of defaulting to recall questions because they're quickest to write.
howTo:
Remember stems: "What is...", "List the...", "Define...", "Which of these is..."
Understand stems: "Explain why...", "Summarize...", "Give an example of...", "Restate in your own words..."
Apply stems: "How would you use... to solve...", "What would happen if you applied... to...", "Show how..."
Analyze stems: "What are the parts of...", "How does... compare to...", "What evidence supports...", "What is the relationship between..."
Evaluate stems: "Which is more effective/valid/justified, and why...", "What criteria would you use to judge...", "Do you agree that... Defend your position."
Create stems: "Design a...", "Propose an alternative...", "Combine... to develop...", "Write a plan for..."
When building a test or assignment, aim for a deliberate spread across levels rather than letting the easiest-to-write recall stems dominate the page — a rough target is fewer than half the items at Remember/Understand.
example: Building a unit assessment, a teacher starts with the last question first — an Evaluate-level item ("Which solution method is most efficient for this type of problem? Defend your answer.") — then works backward, writing Remember and Understand items only for the vocabulary and procedures genuinely needed to access that final question, instead of padding the test with easy recall items first.
sourceName: University of British Columbia, Carl Wieman Science Education Initiative — Question Stems Based on Bloom's Taxonomy

title: Wait Time After Questioning
description: Deliberately pausing 3-5 seconds after asking a question — and again after a student responds — before calling on anyone, giving every student time to think instead of rewarding the fastest hand.
howTo:
Ask the question, then silently count to at least 3-5 seconds before calling on a student.
Resist the urge to fill the silence, rephrase, or call on the first raised hand.
After a student answers, pause again before responding or calling on another student.
Watch for more hands (and more varied hands) rising as the pause continues.
example: After asking "Why did the author choose to end the chapter here?" the teacher counts silently to five, watching more hands slowly rise across the room instead of calling on the first hand up, then calls on a student who was not among the first to raise a hand.
sourceName: Kent State Center for Teaching and Learning

title: Cold-Call: Equitable Participation System
description: A daily routine where the teacher calls on students at random — using sticks, cards, or a name-picker — rather than only on volunteers, so every student stays accountable for being ready to answer.
howTo:
Build a random-call system: popsicle sticks, numbered cards, or a digital randomizer.
Ask the question first, give thinking/wait time, then draw a name.
Return each name to the pool after it's drawn so students know they could be called again at any point.
Keep the tone warm and low-stakes — frame it as "everyone thinks, then I'll pick," not a gotcha.
example: Before discussing the causes of WWI, the teacher asks a question, waits five seconds, then draws a name from a cup of popsicle sticks. Every stick returns to the cup after being drawn, so students know they could be called again at any point and stay prepared throughout the lesson.
sourceName: teacherhead.com (Teach Like a Champion)

title: Costa's Three Levels of Questioning (Science)
description: A three-tier questioning framework — gather, process, apply — that teachers use to move discussion beyond simple data recall into reasoning and transfer, ensuring a class visits all three levels rather than staying at Level 1.
howTo:
Ask Level 1 (Gather) questions answerable by looking at the data or text directly.
Ask Level 2 (Process) questions that require reasoning with the concept to explain why something works the way it does.
Ask Level 3 (Apply) questions asking where the idea matters beyond this case or how a related claim could be tested.
Write at least one question of each level before the lesson and open with a Level 2 or 3 question rather than Level 1.
example: Using the ice-melting phenomenon, the teacher opens with a Level 2 question rather than Level 1: 'Why does the ice on the metal block melt faster even though the metal feels colder to the touch?' A Level 1 gather question follows, asking students to read the percent-melted values directly off the data table at four minutes. Then a Level 3 apply question pushes transfer: 'Where else does this same heat-transfer property matter — for example, why is a cooler made of foam instead of metal?' The teacher writes at least one question at each level before the lesson so the class visits reasoning and transfer, not just recall.
videoTitle: Costa's Levels of Questioning
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: RallyRobin: Possible Interpretations
description: A timed partner-turn-taking structure where students alternate text-based observations and interpretations before the class settles on a reading, so every voice generates possibilities before consensus narrows them. It builds engagement by lowering the risk of a first interpretive attempt and requiring every turn to point to specific textual evidence.
howTo:
Give students 45 seconds of silent annotation before talking.
Have partners alternate one observation or interpretation at a time for 2 minutes, with no repeats, and require every turn to point to a word, image, structural choice, or pattern in the text.
Give partners 1 minute to choose the interpretation worth testing further.
Have each student individually record two different interpretations and circle the one they will defend or revise.
If students retell plot instead of interpreting, require the sentence stem: 'The author's choice of ___ may suggest ___.'
example: Using "The Story of an Hour," partners alternate observations and interpretations for two minutes, each turn pointing to a specific word, image, or pattern, such as the repetition of "free" or the open window imagery. If a student starts retelling the plot instead of interpreting, the teacher requires the stem "The author's choice of ___ may suggest ___," and each student ends by recording two different interpretations and circling the one they will defend.
videoTitle: Rally Robin Kagan Example
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Structured Partner Talk (A/B Roles)
description: A set of printable partner-talk protocols with assigned A/B roles and an 'add or challenge' rule, giving every student rehearsal time and requiring real listening rather than waiting to speak.
howTo:
Assign Partner A and Partner B roles using something visible in the room (e.g., 'the partner closer to the window is A') to avoid wasting time.
Have Partner A speak first (e.g., name the most important repeated word and where it appears).
Require Partner B to add an occurrence A missed or challenge the choice, rather than simply agreeing.
For claim rehearsal, have the partner ask the discipline's question, 'Where does it say so?', which the speaker must answer with a specific line before writing.
For revision, have partners trade the line they are standing on and find the passage that most complicates (not disproves) it, then decide together whether the claim survives, bends, or breaks.
example: Assigned by proximity to the window, Partner A tells Partner B the most important repeated word in "The Story of an Hour" and where it appears, and Partner B must add an occurrence A missed or challenge the choice rather than just agreeing. Later, for revision, partners trade the line they're standing on and find the passage that most complicates — not disproves — it, such as testing a "bad marriage" claim against "she had loved him — sometimes," then decide together whether the claim survives, bends, or breaks.
videoTitle: Talking to a Partner (Interactive Modeling)
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Number Talks
description: A short daily routine where students mentally solve a problem, then share and compare multiple valid strategies for solving it — building number sense and flexible mental math rather than a single memorized procedure.
howTo:
Pose a single problem designed for mental math — no paper or pencil.
Give quiet think time; students show a thumbs-up when ready.
Collect 2-4 different student strategies on the board, in the student's own words.
Ask the class to compare strategies — which was fastest, which makes the most sense, are they all valid?
Keep it short (5-10 minutes) and low-stakes; no grades.
example: The teacher writes "29 + 47" on the board. After a minute of silent thinking, three students share different strategies: rounding 29 up to 30 and adjusting, breaking both numbers into tens and ones, and counting up from 47. The class briefly compares which strategy felt fastest and why all three land on the same answer.
sourceName: NAESP

title: Socratic Seminar
description: A full-period, text-anchored student-led discussion with an inner and outer circle, requiring a marked text and written questions as the entry ticket so preparation — not confidence — determines who can participate, ending with a written revision that cites a classmate's contribution.
howTo:
Require a marked text and three written questions (one at each Costa level) as the entry ticket; unprepared students join the outer circle as process observers.
Open with a student's Level 2 or 3 question, never the teacher's, and seat 12–15 students in an inner circle with an outer circle observing and coaching.
Let the inner circle discuss for about 25 minutes while the teacher sits outside the circle and only intervenes to re-anchor the talk to the text (paragraph and line).
Require posted talk moves: build on, respectfully disagree with evidence, invite a quiet voice in, and return to the text.
At halftime, swap the outer circle in after one minute of coaching from their partner (about 15 minutes).
Close with a written revision of each student's Reader's Sentence in light of the seminar, citing one classmate's point by name.
example: Running a seminar on Kate Chopin's "The Story of an Hour," the teacher opens with a student's Level 3 question about whether the story blames Louise for her joy, then sits outside the inner circle of 12-15 students while they discuss for 25 minutes, intervening only to ask them to return to a paragraph and line. After the outer circle swaps in, the class closes by revising their Reader's Sentence claim in writing, citing a classmate's point by name, as when one student credits a peer's question about why the narrator never judges Louise.
videoTitle: Adapting Socratic Seminars for Elementary Students
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Socratic Seminar → Written Reflection
description: A student-led, text-anchored discussion where a marked/annotated text is the ticket to speak, every claim must return to a specific paragraph, and the seminar closes with each student revising their written claim to cite a classmate's point by name. It boosts achievement by converting talk visibly into writing, proving discussion changed thinking rather than just filled time.
howTo:
Require a marked, annotated text as the entry ticket; unprepared students observe from an outer circle until ready.
Have each student bring written questions at multiple levels of depth (e.g., Costa's three levels) and open with a student's question, not the teacher's.
Run the inner-circle discussion with every claim anchored back to the text by paragraph or line number; the teacher tracks talk but intervenes only to re-anchor to the text.
Require talk moves such as building on, respectfully disagreeing with evidence, and inviting quieter voices in.
Close with a written revision of each student's claim that explicitly cites a classmate's point by name, showing the discussion changed the writing.
example: Before a seminar on Kate Chopin's 'The Story of an Hour,' each student marks up the text and brings three written questions, one at each Costa level, since the marked text is the ticket to sit in the inner circle. A student opens with a Level 2 question about why the narrator never judges Louise Mallard, and the discussion runs student-to-student with every claim anchored to a paragraph number, the teacher intervening only to redirect back to the text. Afterward, each student revises their own written interpretation and must cite a specific classmate's point: for example, crediting a peer named Marcus whose question about the narrator's refusal to condemn Louise changed their reading of the ending.
videoTitle: Scaffolding Discussion Skills With a Socratic Circle
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Philosophical Chairs
description: A structured debate where two facing rows argue a binary claim, speakers must paraphrase the previous speaker before responding, and students may change seats mid-debate as long as they can name the argument that moved them — making changing one's mind from evidence the explicit goal.
howTo:
Post one genuinely arguable binary claim and set up chairs in two facing rows (agree/disagree) with a small undecided section.
Have each student silently write their position and one named source before sitting (3 minutes).
Run alternating speakers, one at a time, requiring each speaker to paraphrase the previous speaker to their satisfaction before responding (12 minutes).
Allow students to change seats whenever a speaker moves them, as long as they can name the argument that moved them.
Require undecided students to choose a side by the close, then have all students write a closing statement naming their position, source, and the strongest argument against them.
example: For the binary claim "The reformers' stated purpose deserves to be taken seriously," two facing rows of chairs argue agree versus disagree, and no student may respond until they paraphrase the previous speaker to that speaker's satisfaction. Students change seats mid-debate whenever an argument moves them, then write a closing statement naming their final position, their source, and the strongest argument raised against them.
videoTitle: Instructional Strategy: Philosophical Chairs
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Structured Academic Controversy
description: Pairs argue an assigned side of a debate from documents, then switch and argue the reverse side without reusing arguments, before dropping roles to write a consensus claim that survives both cases — making disagreement the engine of deeper reading.
howTo:
Assign each pair a side to argue (not their own opinion) so students must read sources supporting a position they may not hold.
Give 8 minutes where every argument must carry a source, date, and verb — no unsourced argument counts.
Have pairs switch sides and argue the reverse without reusing their opponent's arguments, forcing a second pass through the document set.
Have pairs drop roles and write one consensus claim that survives everything argued, naming evidence on both sides and specifying "for whom" and "when" if the answer is "both".
example: Arguing the Dawes Act's effects, pairs are assigned a side to defend using the document set, then must switch and argue the reverse without reusing their opponent's points, hunting the sources a second time for what they missed. Finally the pair drops roles and writes one consensus claim — for example, that allotment could be both sincerely intended and destructive at once — naming evidence from both the Mohonk proceedings and Chitto Harjo's testimony.
videoTitle: Steps of Structured Academic Controversy
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: The Tribunal
description: A mock-trial structure that puts a policy (never a people) on trial, with advocates, witnesses presenting numbered exhibits, and jurors who must cite specific exhibits in their verdicts — turning corroboration into courtroom drama grounded strictly in the document set.
howTo:
Assign roles: advocates for the policy, advocates against, witnesses who present exhibits, and jurors with verdict forms; build cases from the document set only, with every argument keyed to an exhibit number (Day 1).
Run opening statements (2 minutes each).
Have witnesses present exhibits while the other side may cross-examine the sourcing — who made it, when, why (20 minutes).
Run closings (2 minutes each).
Have jurors deliberate aloud and deliver verdicts that cite the two exhibits that decided the case and name one complicating exhibit (10 minutes).
example: The class puts the allotment policy itself on trial: advocates for the policy cite the Lake Mohonk proceedings and the Act's title, advocates against call the acreage records and Chitto Harjo's 1906 testimony as witnesses, and jurors deliver verdicts that must cite the two exhibits that decided the case plus one complicating exhibit. The teacher reminds the room, "You may attack an exhibit's sourcing, its context, or its scope. You may not attack a people, and you may not invent evidence."
videoTitle: Making Arguments Based on Evidence: Mock Trials
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Hot Seat / Press Conference
description: One student role-plays a historical figure using a document-based dossier while the class asks sourced questions; the figure may only answer what the documents support, revealing the limits of a historical perspective without lapsing into caricature.
howTo:
Build one-page dossiers for figures connected to the documents, listing only what each figure could plausibly know, want, and cite.
Have a volunteer (or the teacher, the first time) take the seat with 2 minutes of prep.
Have the class ask sourced questions that must cite something from the document set (10 minutes).
Require the seat to answer only what the dossier and documents support, allowing "my figure wouldn't know that" as a valid answer.
Debrief out of role on what the figure could not see from their position (5 minutes).
example: One student takes the hot seat as a Dawes Commission enrollment clerk, working from a one-page dossier built only from the document set, while classmates ask sourced questions like "The acreage records document three million acres sold: how do you explain that?" The seat may only answer what the dossier supports, and "my figure wouldn't know that" is treated as a valid, instructive answer during the out-of-role debrief on what the clerk's position couldn't let him see.
videoTitle: Hot Seating
sourceName: The Turner Guide to Student Engagement — Paul Turner

title: Student-Led Discussions
description: When students disengage, hand over most of the discussion to them to assess and rebuild understanding.
howTo: Pose a question and step back, letting students carry the conversation and build on each other's ideas while you listen for gaps in understanding.
example: Partway through a Socratic seminar on The Crucible, the teacher notices students have gone quiet and are just waiting to be called on, so instead of jumping back in, the teacher poses one open question — "Who in this play do you actually blame for what happens to Tituba?" — and steps back from the circle entirely. Students pick up the thread themselves, building on and challenging each other's claims for the next ten minutes while the teacher only takes notes on gaps in reasoning. The teacher waits until the conversation stalls again before re-entering with a targeted follow-up question.
videoTitle: Using Discussions to Inspire Active Participation in Learning
sourceName: Renaissance

title: Costa's Levels of Questioning: A Faster Companion to Bloom's
description: Planning six Bloom's tiers works well ahead of time, but it's a lot to track live during a discussion. Costa's three levels — Gathering, Processing, Applying — map onto the same cognitive climb with fewer categories, which is why many teachers reach for Costa's in the moment and save Bloom's six tiers for lesson planning.
howTo:
Level 1 (Gathering) folds in Bloom's Remember and Understand: information stated directly in the text or material. Power verbs: define, describe, identify, list, recall, restate.
Level 2 (Processing) folds in Bloom's Apply and Analyze: reasoning with the information rather than just retrieving it. Power verbs: compare, infer, classify, distinguish, explain why.
Level 3 (Applying) folds in Bloom's Evaluate and Create: using the information beyond the immediate example. Power verbs: judge, predict, hypothesize, design, justify, generalize.
Use Bloom's six tiers when you're planning a full lesson in advance and want to be deliberate about hitting every rung.
Switch to Costa's three levels during live discussion, when you need a quick mental check rather than a six-category rubric.
example: A teacher still writes out all six Bloom's-level questions in advance for lesson planning. But once the discussion is live, they track only three floors in their head: did we open with a gathering question, did we get students processing (comparing, inferring), and did we reach an applying question (predicting, justifying)? That three-item mental checklist is fast enough to run in real time, which the full six-tier version usually isn't.
videoTitle: Costa's Levels of Questioning
sourceName: Edutopia — Stirring Students to Ask Tougher Questions (Costa's Levels vs. Bloom's Taxonomy)

title: Blackburn's Three-Part Definition of Rigor
description: Barbara Blackburn's widely used definition reframes rigor as three conditions that all have to be true at once, not a difficulty dial: high expectations for every student, real support to reach them, and evidence that they actually got there. Miss any one of the three and it isn't rigor — it's just hard, just nice, or just busy.
howTo:
Check a task against all three parts, not just one: are expectations genuinely high for this student rather than quietly lowered ahead of time; is there real scaffolding — modeling, graphic organizers, guided practice — to help reach that expectation; does the task require the student to demonstrate the learning, not just complete it.
Watch for common myths that masquerade as rigor: more homework isn't automatically more rigorous — quantity without quality is busywork; lowering the bar for a struggling student isn't kindness, it removes their access to rigor they could reach with support; owning a rigorous-sounding textbook, program, or piece of technology doesn't guarantee rigor — how it's used does.
Rewrite one existing assignment by raising cognitive demand without adding length — for example, turn a true/false quiz into one where every false statement must be rewritten as a true one and cited back to the text.
Extend the same idea to younger grades: for K–2, rigor can be as simple as consistently following an answer with “How do you know?” or “Why?” instead of moving on.
example: A teacher notices a true/false worksheet on cell structure feels easy for some students and frustrating for others. Instead of making two versions — an “easy” one and a “hard” one — she keeps one worksheet for the whole class but changes the task: for every statement marked false, students rewrite it so it's true and cite the textbook page that supports the correction. Same content, same time, genuinely more rigorous for every student in the room.
videoTitle: What Is Rigor?
sourceName: Victorian Department of Education (Academy) — "Ten Myths About Rigor," Barbara R. Blackburn, Ph.D.

title: Quality Over Quantity: Never Work Harder Than Your Students
description: Robyn Jackson's principle names a specific version of the difficulty trap: teachers who equate great teaching with constant, exhausting effort — grading piles, elaborate materials, doing the thinking out loud for students — often end up working harder than the students do. Rigor means flipping that ratio so the cognitive lifting happens on the student side of the desk.
howTo:
For one assignment, notice who's doing the thinking: if you're the one summarizing, explaining, and connecting ideas while students copy or listen, the rigor is happening in your head, not theirs.
Redesign the task so students do that thinking instead — have them explain why an answer is correct to a partner or in writing rather than you explaining it; have them infer a vocabulary word's meaning from context before you pre-teach it.
Apply a quality-over-quantity check before assigning work: could this task be shorter and still require the same depth of thinking? If a 20-question worksheet and a 5-question worksheet require the same reasoning, assign the shorter one.
Watch for “helping” that removes the struggle entirely — support means scaffolding the climb, not carrying the student up it.
example: A teacher planning a unit review realizes she's spent three nights building an elaborate study guide that answers every possible test question in advance. She scraps it and instead gives students the list of topics and 15 minutes of class time to build their own study guide in pairs using their notes. She still assesses the same content mastery, but the students did the organizing and synthesizing she used to do for them.
videoTitle: Never Work Harder Than Your Students: Great Teaching Principles
sourceName: ASCD — Never Work Harder Than Your Students and Other Principles of Great Teaching (Robyn R. Jackson)

title: Ditch the Worksheet: A Rigor-First Alternative
description: A worksheet can look like rigor — it fills class time and produces a stack of papers — while actually asking students to do very little real thinking: locate an answer, copy a definition, fill a blank someone else already organized. Replacing worksheets with student-built visual thinking (sketchnotes, thinking maps, open-ended questions) puts the genuine cognitive work — deciding what matters and how ideas connect — back on the student, which is the actual test of rigor from Chapter 3.
howTo:
Before assigning a worksheet, ask: is the student finding an answer, or building understanding? If it's the former, look for a visual-thinking swap instead.
Teach a simple thinking map (bubble map for describing, flow map for sequencing, double-bubble map for comparing) and have students construct their own rather than filling in a pre-made organizer — the construction itself is the rigor.
Pair the map with genuine open-ended questions that have no single located answer: "How do stripes help this animal during a storm?" or "What would happen if this step were skipped?" rather than "Fill in the blank."
Use the finished map as a discussion starter, not a grading checklist — ask students to defend a choice they made on their own map to a partner.
example: After reading a story about an animal surviving a storm, instead of a worksheet asking students to list three facts about the animal, a teacher has students build their own bubble map: a center circle labeled with the animal's situation, with radiating bubbles the student fills in themselves — strong legs, sharp claws, striped fur, hiding in thick plants. The teacher then asks, "How do stripes help during a storm?" and "What other animals might struggle more in the same storm?" — questions a worksheet's answer key could never have anticipated, because the students generated the content the questions are about.
videoTitle: Building a Language for Learning: Introducing Thinking Maps
sourceName: ASCD Educational Leadership — "Ditch the Worksheets!"
